extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of British television and media criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative points one might use to judge a single British television drama (here: Dennis Potter's Blackeyes), covering theme, production, style, reception, controversy and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and articulation of central theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Potter described the series's theme as the objectification of "young and attractive women as consumer goods in a way that brutalises both sexes".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the programme clearly communicates its stated thematic intent (objectification/consumerism/sexism), whether scenes and narrative choices illustrate that theme, and whether critics/audiences can perceive that intention (the page documents disagreement between Potter's aim and critics' perceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of sensitive subject matter (child abuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Potter attempted to address his own experience of child abuse in Blackeyes; some critics overlooked this element while others (Sunday Telegraph) acknowledged it as the source of harrowing material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether traumatic material is handled responsibly and comprehensibly, whether voiceover or narrative framing makes the context clear, and whether the intended psychological/emotional purpose of such scenes is communicated to viewers rather than being obscured by controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount and presentation of sexual content and nudity
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of the British press reacted negatively, highlighting the amount of sex and nudity — early previews called it "soft porn" and 'a simple turn-on for male viewers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether sexual content serves dramatic/critical purposes or appears gratuitous, whether it aligns with stated thematic aims, and how presentation (framing, editing, camera work) affects perception (titillating vs diagnostic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of women and accusations of objectification/sexism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics accused Potter of a 'twisted attitude to women', calling him 'a very sick man' and accusing the series of feeding what it claimed to diagnose; Potter defended that explicit scenes were not intended to titillate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether female characters are depicted as objects/consumer goods versus as fully-drawn characters, whether narrative voice or camera perspective sexualizes them, and whether the work critiques or perpetuates institutionalized sexism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and risk-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reviewers (e.g., Mark Lawson) applauded Potter's willingness to take risks and described the work as possibly his most interesting and original since previous acclaimed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate innovation in form, narrative, or subject matter and whether riskiness contributes to artistic value or merely alienates audiences; consider comparisons with an author's earlier work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative coherence and complexity (number of strands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Potter later admitted there were 'too many strands' and that the style was alienating; he blamed excessive strands and execution in part for the failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether multiple narrative threads cohere into a comprehensible whole, whether complexity serves meaning, or whether overcomplexity fragments audience engagement (anti-pattern: too many unresolved strands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone, style and accessibility (alienating vs engaging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics and Potter himself described the style as 'alienating', 'abstruse', 'deliberately uncomfortable' and densely imagined; Potter said the style alienated viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge consistency of tone, whether stylistic choices (fragmentation, voiceover, discomfort) achieve intended effects, and whether style obstructs understanding or provokes productive responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction and the creator's role (author directing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Potter directed the series himself (the only time he did so for TV) despite illness; he later said he would consider it a mistake to direct the serial himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the director (especially when also writer/creator) makes beneficial or detrimental choices, whether wearing multiple creative hats harmed objectivity/execution, and whether direction realized or undermined the script's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production values and technical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC awarded a budget of £2.4 million; it was shot on 35 mm film and took 18 months to complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cinematography, film stock/format choices, production design and whether the production budget and technical execution support the narrative and thematic ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performances and casting
rubrics_metrics.description: Cast included Gina Bellman as the title character with Michael Gough in a key role; the page lists principal cast without extended performance critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lead and supporting performances for credibility, range and fit with the material; consider whether casting choices reinforce or undermine themes (e.g., modelling industry depiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-broadcast publicity and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: The series was promoted (cover of The Listener, interviews on chat shows and in newspapers) and Potter repeatedly framed it as personal, saying he was 'falling in love with Blackeyes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how marketing, interviews and pre-release framing shape expectations and critical reception; premature hyperbole or provocative promotion can prime hostile readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception vs intended meaning (misreading risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: A press screening provoked negative responses and scathing tabloid coverage; Potter felt critics missed aspects of his intent (e.g., the child-abuse element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the gap between authorial intent and public/critical interpretation, and whether the work communicates its aims clearly enough to avoid being misread as endorsing what it critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public controversy, tabloid reaction and reputation management
rubrics_metrics.description: The series spawned tabloid cartoons, derisive nicknames ('Dirty Den'), and sustained tabloid polemic leading Potter to a low point personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how controversial content leads to public backlash, the role of tabloids in shaping reputation, and whether the creators/institution managed controversy responsibly or exacerbated it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longevity, availability and critical reassessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackeyes practically vanished after its original airing, was repeated on niche channels in the 90s/00s, remains unreleased on DVD/Blu-ray, and later critics have called for reassessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the work's significance endures, is subject to re-evaluation over time, and whether limited availability affects cultural memory and scholarly reassessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between provocation and clarity of argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Some defenders argue explicit scenes were intended diagnostically rather than to titillate, while critics saw them as gratuitous; Potter acknowledged the style was 'so successful it alienated every fucking person who ever saw it'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether provocative elements advance a coherent critical argument or merely shock; examine whether provocation is justified by clarity of the work's thesis or undermines it.
